title: Culture Is What We Feed
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer argues that culture is not a mission statement or a list of values but what becomes normal between people: what we reward, tolerate, encourage, and repeatedly practice. Although institutions shape us from the outside, each person also brings attention, assumptions, silence, and care into a space, and all of that becomes part of the culture. When enough people withdraw their attention and participation, a vacuum forms, and vacuums get filled by whoever is willing to show up. She uses anxiety about artificial intelligence as an example of a cultural question about who participates and whose values guide development. Her practical invitation is to start closer to home by noticing what we personally feed, whether fear or possibility, cynicism or curiosity, competition or contribution. The post ends with reflection questions for leaders about what their groups reinforce and what quality they want to bring deliberately.
points: Culture is the behaviour a group makes normal through what it rewards, tolerates, and repeatedly practises, not what is written on the wall.
Every person carries expectations, attention, and willingness to speak or stay silent into a space, and those contributions shape the culture.
When thoughtful people disengage, they leave a vacuum that others fill, so withdrawal is itself a cultural choice.
Questions such as who gets to decide how AI develops are cultural as much as technological, and they depend on who participates.
Change can begin by becoming clear about what you personally feed, and small repeated choices can shift a whole system.
quotes: Culture is not the mission statement on the wall. It is not the values listed on the website or the things we say we believe when everyone is behaving well.
Culture is what becomes normal between us. It is what we reward, what we tolerate, what we encourage and what we repeatedly practice.
When enough of us withdraw our attention, our care and our participation, we leave a vacuum. And vacuums get filled.
So perhaps changing culture is not quite as abstract as it appears. We do not have to begin by changing everyone. We can begin by becoming clearer about what we ourselves are feeding.
Are we feeding fear or possibility? Cynicism or curiosity? Exhaustion or care? Competition or contribution?
There is no lasting thriving at the expense of everyone else.
Culture may change this way more often than we recognize, not through one sweeping transformation, but through what enough of us repeatedly choose to nurture, protect and keep alive together.
